### 2.10 Niklas Hidman — TC study, results and candid Q&A (ID 10), continued

**Method and design logic.** The study's aim is stated as enhancing borehole heat transfer to improve heat pump efficiency, with borehole thermal resistance simplified as resistances in series R_tot = R_w + R_p + R_f, and the brine convective term R_f amounting to "about 50% of the total heat transfer resistance" at certain operating conditions (`tr-10-002` 00:04:09; `deck-s18`). Operating window: fluctuating heat demand gives collector Reynolds numbers roughly 1300–3300, smooth-pipe transition ≈2300, so both laminar and unsteady flow occur in service (`tr-10-003` 00:05:43; `deck-s19`). Laminar ⇒ brine is ~50% of total borehole resistance; unsteady ⇒ heat transfer 5–10× higher and the brine term falls to ~5% (`tr-10-004` 00:06:52; `deck-s19`). Hence: "we clearly have most to gain by enhancing the convective heat transfer … below 2300" (`tr-10-004`).

**Design trade-off, stated as a constraint, not a result.** Fins must trigger unsteadiness as low in Re as possible without raising pressure drop much above Re 2300; "the maximum of about 10% increase at [Reynolds] numbers above 2300 is the maximum that we can allow. Otherwise … the net gain of introducing fins diminishes" (`tr-10-005`–`tr-10-006` 00:09:09; `deck-s21`). Manufacturability and cost are named as a third criterion in the same slide (`deck-s21`).

**Method.** Fully resolved 3D Direct Numerical Simulation — "you directly solve the fluid and energy conservation equations… there are no modelling involved here", at high spatial/temporal resolution and high computational cost (`tr-10-006`–`tr-10-007` 00:10:26; `deck-s22`). Inputs: Re, Pr, parametrised pipe geometry; outputs: Nusselt number and friction factor (`tr-10-007`–`tr-10-008` 00:11:35). Validation: grid independence (Nu and f invariant under refinement) plus comparison with analytical laminar and experimental turbulent correlations for smooth pipes, which the presenter reports matching closely (`tr-10-008`–`tr-10-010` 00:14:14; `deck-s23`, `deck-s52` — base grid 116 cells/D). He flags a genuine limit: near transition "there are no experimental correlations that are universally valid. It's a tricky, very tricky region" (`tr-10-010`).

**Four-step procedure and quantitative findings** (`tr-10-010`–`tr-10-016`; `deck-s24`–`deck-s30`):
1. *Strategy.* Straight, continuous-helical, alternating-helical fins, compared at common parameters D = 40 mm inner, 16 fins, 0.6 mm height, one revolution per ~0.7 m (`tr-10-011` 00:15:26; `deck-s25`). Unsteadiness persisted down to Re 2050 (straight), 1950 (continuous) and "somewhere between 1700 and 1800" (alternating) — "clearly the most promising design" (`tr-10-012` 00:18:00).
2. *Fin height,* alternating design, Re 3300, heights 0→1.8 mm: friction factor rises steeply above ~1 mm; "somewhere below 1mm fin heights will give a very minor effect on the pressure drop at high Reynolds numbers" (`tr-10-013`–`tr-10-014` 00:19:15; `deck-s27` adds 10–20% heat-transfer enhancement at that Re, already high for smooth pipe).
3. *Fin count* (2, 16, 24, 32), 0.6 mm: 16 and 2 both induce unsteadiness down to ~1700–1800; 24 and 32 do not, because "they probably come too close to each other… the flow will probably just pass by on the outside of the fins". Conclusion: more than 16 is not advantageous, and two fins already alter the flow significantly (`tr-10-014`–`tr-10-015` 00:20:37; `deck-s28`).
4. *Twist rate,* period 1.4 m: 0° = straight; performance improves to about 45°, and 45/180/360° perform "more or less the same" — "at least 45° is suitable and this is not a lot. So it's quite surprising" (`tr-10-016` 00:21:54; `deck-s29`).

**Promising design and comparison.** More than 30 fin designs evaluated by DNS including preliminary tests (`tr-10-016`; `deck-s30`). Promising design: alternating helical, 0.6 mm, 16 fins, 360° per ~0.7 m. Versus smooth pipe: earlier transition in the friction curve; "about 3 to 600% better convective heat transfer in the intermediate region of about 1700 to 2300"; "just a few percent or even less higher pressure drop outside of this region" (`tr-10-019` 00:25:45; `deck-s31`, `deck-s33`). Pr was varied ~20–75 to represent different brines (`tr-10-017` 00:23:22).

**Q&A — the candid content.**

- *Non-optimality, explicitly conceded.* Asked whether 360°/0.7 m was the optimum: "I cannot say it's an optimum, but it's one of the best" (`tr-10-023`–`tr-10-024` 00:32:28). This directly qualifies the marketing deck's claim that the study "shows that MuoviTech's patented fin design with alternating fin direction is the optimal solution" (`deck-s12`, `deck-s13`) and the narration's "most optimal heat transfer" (`tr-13-000`). The research deck's own wording is "promising design" (`deck-s30`, `deck-s33`).
- *Untested combinations.* "There are many parameters and if you start to tweak one and then two, then you don't really know what is happening anymore… you would like in a perfect world to do 1000 simulations covering all different combinations but with realistic cost and timeline" — a hypothesis-led, one-dimension-at-a-time search (`tr-10-024`). Explicitly untested: two fins at 45° and 0.6 mm — "not that exact combination we're not looked at" (`tr-10-027` 00:36:04). Also raised as future work: fewer fins with greater height (`tr-10-025` 00:33:30), and an 8–10 fin study (`tr-10-040` 00:51:41, answered "yes we can make that study").
- *Diminishing returns above 2300.* "We shouldn't focus on the fluid resistance then… even with a smooth pipe, the resistance is only 5% of the total borehole resistance… if we decrease that 1% more it doesn't really give much effect" (`tr-10-025`).
- *Fluid dependence.* Same Re and Pr ⇒ same f and Nu; changing fluid moves the Reynolds number, so "you have to go back and look in those plots" (`tr-10-029`–`tr-10-030` 00:39:36). Higher Pr ⇒ larger fin benefit; Pr 75 associated with ~33% propylene glycol, ethanol lower, ethylene glycol lowest of those named (`tr-10-030`–`tr-10-031` 00:41:05 — the ASR here is garbled and the fluid-to-Pr mapping should be re-checked). Water: Pr ≈ 6–7, low viscosity, so "the flow rate will not go so low that the water will become laminar, not in these systems" (`tr-10-032`–`tr-10-033` 00:43:24). A participant notes water-only systems are "quite common" in the Netherlands, and the group reasons that water does not abolish the window but shifts it, with the caveat that Central European systems may be designed below Re 2300 even at maximum flow (`tr-10-034` 00:44:32). Counter-argument recorded: water forces extra borehole metres to keep above 0 °C at the heat pump (`tr-10-035` 00:45:50). **This is an argumentation rehearsal, not a product decision.**
- *Double U.* "If they are less than 1700, you would have no gain with the TurboCollector. But as long as you're within that window, you still have the benefit"; and the deeper objection — with a double collector "when you run the system at Max, you're in the laminar… that's going to push down the temperature a lot… making the whole of the [SCOP] very bad" (`tr-10-037`–`tr-10-038` 00:48:02).
- *Production variants by country.* The reference design shown is "more or less the Swedish" die head, twisted 360°; "in Finland you're twisting it 180. But as the study shows it works both ways", so "we don't need the … CapEx investment that we discussed earlier" (`tr-10-022`–`tr-10-023` 00:30:53). A UK description of "15 very small fins … straight for about 1m then twists and then straight again" is put in the chat and answered "no, that's not right" (`tr-10-023`). Fin counts across variants are "within the range of 15 or 16", heights differ slightly, "all of them is within the scope what works", and realignment is "a really small cost and small investment" (`tr-10-023`). Patent: "We have optionality in the patent" (`tr-10-021` 00:28:23); `deck-s05` states the alternating helical design is patented.
- *Material cost and price.* Extra material for 16 fins vs smooth: "I don't remember … it was like 3%" (`tr-10-029` 00:38:20); later "like 4% or something like that. Three I think… three additional between 2 and 16 — oh between smooth" — the speakers themselves do not settle it (`tr-10-041` 00:53:06). Halving fin count saves "1–2%" (`tr-10-041`). Commercially: "we can't say these things to the market … they are not willing to pay for the turbo — cost is not the question for the customer"; and "we have different price strategies between the different countries because my turbo price is the same price as my [smooth], but still customers don't want it" (`tr-10-041`, `tr-10-052` 01:05:51). A proposal to produce only TurboCollector is rejected on margin grounds: where turbo is not specified, "we're competing with the smooth price from the competitor with the turbo price from us. We can't really take that extra margin" (`tr-10-051`–`tr-10-052`).
- *Competitor opinion.* On a Johnson-group "shark collector" with many straight fins covering roughly half the surface: "we thought this is a turbo … the study shows that it creates laminar flows and I've read that paper. This is actually what they're saying, that they're blocking turbulence… they're saying you get lower pressure drop… if you have lower pressure drop, you have lower heat transfer. So it's an anti-turbo… basically fooling people… most likely a really crappy product" (`tr-10-042`–`tr-10-043` 00:54:20). **Recorded internal opinion of a named competitor, partly based on reading the competitor's paper; not an independent test.**
- *Limits on tuning whole systems.* Asked whether the findings open an aftermarket service of adjusting flow rates on installed turbo systems: lowering flow also raises ΔT at the heat pump heat exchanger, "which could be bad for the COP", so "it would be tricky to go into that area"; "is plausible… but we don't have the knowledge for it right now. I think you need a complete system understanding in order to tweak an existing … system and claim you have done it better" (`tr-10-043`–`tr-10-046` 00:56:58). Also recorded: most domestic heat pumps regulate flow, commercial ones often step-regulate compressors, and one supplier reportedly installs a separate non-regulating circulation pump (`tr-10-044`–`tr-10-045`).
- *Pressure-drop penalty quantified in discussion.* The single worst observed data point above the window is agreed as ~2%: "we're saying pretty much zero. And the maximum observed in one data point is 2%… I think 2% in a simulation like this is within the error margin" (`tr-10-049`–`tr-10-051` 01:03:49).

### 2.11 Pressure-drop tool demo and Q&A (ID 12)

**Framing.** An "introduction … not meant to be proper training", recorded, questions in chat, following the previous day's Signhild session; the tool replaces an Excel file with a web app (`tr-12-000` 00:00:04). 

**Pump curves.** Y axis available pressure in kPa, X axis flow in l/s, red curves for pump capacity fractions (40%…100%). Worked illustration: 3 l/s at 40 kPa needs ~80% capacity; at 60 kPa ~100%; at 100 kPa the pump cannot deliver 3 l/s and the operating point slides back to ≈2.2 l/s (`tr-12-001`–`tr-12-003` 00:05:42).

**Inputs and worked examples.** Required: distance house→borehole top, borehole/collector depth, dimensions, flow rate, fluid (`tr-12-004` 00:07:11). Tool location: web page → Info Service → Calculation → Pressure drop; login required; "new project" (`tr-12-004`–`tr-12-005` 00:08:41). Single-house example: 200 m collector, 40 mm, smooth, SDR 17, one borehole, 10 m horizontal 40 mm SDR 17, no main pipe, 1 l/s, 28% ethanol ⇒ 250 kPa (`tr-12-006`–`tr-12-007` 00:12:01). Outputs below the graph: flow per collector, Reynolds number, total borehole metres (`tr-12-008` 00:13:32). Adding a second borehole at constant total flow *reduces* pressure drop to well under half, because flow per loop halves (`tr-12-008`–`tr-12-009` 00:15:41).

**Balancing.** With unequal borehole lengths, the short loop takes more flow, shifting energy extraction unevenly; balancing valves are closed until the added drop equals the missing pipe's drop, so "the pressure drop in a system … with a balancing valve will be the same as if all boreholes were the same length". Design rule: size on the highest-pressure-drop loop (`tr-12-010`–`tr-12-011` 00:19:00).

**Manifold case and sizing against the heat pump.** Two boreholes into a manifold chamber, 50 m horizontal + 50 m main pipe, 1 l/s combined ⇒ choose a larger main pipe (75 mm) ⇒ 98 kPa (`tr-12-013`–`tr-12-014` 00:23:39). Limits come from the consultant or the heat pump data sheet; a NIBE table example gives nominal 3.1 l/s and 65 kPa external available pressure (`tr-12-014`–`tr-12-015` 00:25:23). Iteration shown: 40 mm too high; 45 mm gives 59 kPa; 50 mm lowers drop but pushes Re below 2300 — resolved by ticking TurboCollector, valid to Re 1800 (`tr-12-016`–`tr-12-017` 00:28:34).

**The nine-minute customer call.** A consultant phoned during slide preparation: 8 boreholes × 250 m, 40 mm SDR 17, 10 m manifold-to-borehole, 50 m of 110 mm main pipe, two heat pumps at 2.09 and 3.1 l/s ⇒ 5.19 l/s combined; target ≤65 kPa. As specified: 159 kPa. Changing to 50 mm brought it below 65 kPa; then, noting that at part load flow falls and the system goes laminar below ~4.1 l/s, whereas TurboCollector holds to ~3.3 l/s, the consultant chose turbo. "This phone call… took 9 minutes." Commercial outcome as stated: contribution margin on collectors would have been 21,000 with smooth 40 mm, and rose to 42,006 with 50 mm turbo — "We actually doubled our profits and the customer got a system that worked" (`tr-12-017`–`tr-12-020` 00:33:36). **The currency is not stated and "42,006" is likely an ASR corruption of a round figure; treat the exact amounts as unknown, the doubling as the speaker's claim.**

**Single vs double loops.** A chart compares single turbo 45, single turbo 40 and double smooth 32: the double 32 does reach the lowest borehole resistance but only at high flow; below that the singles are better (`tr-12-020`–`tr-12-021` 00:35:39). Applied to the 8×250 m case, 32 mm doubles loop count to 16, Re 2248 with turbo but laminar without, and pressure drop too high for the heat pump either way (`tr-12-021`–`tr-12-022` 00:37:13). A Central-European variant — 125 m × 32 boreholes — gives very low pressure drop but Reynolds far too low even in SDR 11 and even with turbo; the recommended alternative is 16 single 40 mm turbo loops, giving low drop and Re above 1800 (`tr-12-022`–`tr-12-024` 00:40:43).

**Reports.** "Download report" produces a PDF with the graph, the data (kPa, flow etc.) and a material list — in the example 16 × 125 m 40 mm TurboCollector plus brine volume and similar items (`tr-12-024` 00:41:00).

**Assumptions, omissions and stated limits.**
- Carried over from the Excel tool: **2.5 kPa flat allowance for the U-bend** and a **10% safety margin** justified by extrusion tolerances (calculation assumes nominal wall) — "that is covering some of these unexpected pressure drops" (`tr-12-029` 00:48:56).
- **No manifold pressure drop** is modelled: "it would be too complicated to add and this is something that the consultants or the companies should add themselves. What is the K_VS value for the valves, for instance?" (`tr-12-030` 00:50:50).
- **Lengths are one-way**: "if the actual distance between the manifold and the borehole is 100 metre, you're clicking 100 metre, you don't click in 200" (`tr-12-030`). A participant asks for on-screen clarification; the answer is a plan to write an explanation page (`tr-12-031` 00:52:18).
- **One manifold only**: "we can only work with one manifold chamber… so far I would say that we have a restriction in how large system we could calculate" (`tr-12-033` 00:54:44).
- **The heat pump sets the flow**: "this is a 60 kilowatt heat pump and it clearly states it needs 3.1 litres, no matter if it's a TurboCollector or a smooth or a double or whatever" — so switching to turbo does not mean existing installations are over-flowed; for very large systems consultants may fix a system flow independently (`tr-12-033`–`tr-12-035` 00:58:10).
- Double collectors are entered by doubling the borehole count; a single/double tick box is only a request for the next version (`tr-12-031`–`tr-12-032` 00:53:22).

**Admin, distribution, roadmap (recorded as status or intention — do not read as delivered features).** Live on the group and Swedish pages only, with a plan to publish on all pages "within a week" (`tr-12-004`). An admin panel lists users; already visible is an external HVAC consultant (named in `tr-12-025` 00:44:06) who had done several calculations, prompting a sales-follow-up idea; "in this first version we don't work with that yet, but we save everything", and per-country e-mail lists can be extracted (`tr-12-025`–`tr-12-026`). MuoviEllipse 55 and 63 are in the dimension list; E-turbo is *not* yet an option and is listed as a possible addition (`tr-12-026`–`tr-12-027` 00:45:32). Heat pump curve overlay exists in code but the selector was removed pending manufacturer permission to use their data (`tr-12-027`–`tr-12-028` 00:47:14). Requested for a later version: per-section and per-metre pressure drop (`tr-12-028`), manifold losses, single/double tick box, an explanation page. One week of internal testing before wider publication and before LinkedIn/social sharing (`tr-12-032` 00:53:22). One Reynolds-number discrepancy raised by e-mail was deferred to a follow-up call (`tr-12-035`–`tr-12-036` 01:00:00).

### 2.12 TC narration (ID 13)

A ~1 min 46 s marketing voice-over. It adds no new technical data beyond the deck and study; its value is as evidence of the **public-facing claim set and its wording**: fully turbulent at maximum load; smooth probe goes laminar at part load; TurboCollector "continue[s] to be turbulent at reduced flow rates"; "Independent research has shown that MuoviTech's unique and patented fin design with alternating fin directions is creating the most optimal heat transfer"; "up to 600% increase in heat transfer"; "negligible pressure drop difference … outside of Reynolds numbers 1800 to 2300"; 50+ year benefit (`tr-13-000`, `tr-13-001` 00:01:16). Note the drift from the source: the study's `deck-s33` says "+300-600% *convective* heat transfer", the narration says "heat transfer"; and "most optimal" conflicts with `tr-10-024` ("I cannot say it's an optimum").

### 2.13 Supporting local decks, script and formulas

- **`TurboCollector presentation.pptx`.** Slides 2–15 are the marketing layer; 17–33 are the Chalmers deck; 51–55 an appendix. Unique knowledge added: the quantified claim chain "turbulent flow at 22% lower flow rates → 80% reduced fluid resistance → **up to** 3.6 °C increase in brine temperature → **up to** 11% COP improvement" (`deck-s07`, `deck-s08`); the annual-exposure estimate that the 1800–2300 window corresponds to "likely ~20% of total annual added kWh" for a typical NIBE pump (`deck-s14`); "SKZ approved", available in all relevant dimensions, "Cons: None" (`deck-s15`); product range data — 32/40/45/50 mm, SDR 11 and 17, lengths to 500 m, MuoviXpert to 70 °C, chambers for 2–20 connections, Magnelis C5 cabinets (`deck-s41`–`deck-s43`, `deck-s36`); and 2017 turnover EUR 25 million in a speaker note (`deck-s40`). **Distinguish sharply:** 3.6 °C and 11% are "up to" maxima; the appendix derivation at `deck-s53` works a different point — "COP … improves with about 3% per 1 °C" giving "about 6.6%", i.e. ~2.2 K at that condition; and `deck-s14` implies the window applies only part of the year. None of these is an annual SPF measurement, and none is a field measurement.
- **`Speaker and Bulletpoints.docx`.** The narration script with on-screen text and a YouTube link (`script-scene0`). Adds the explicit on-screen numbers 11% COP, 22% lower flow rates, 80% reduced thermal fluid resistance, 3.6 °C, 600%, and "Study made in cooperation with Chalmers University in Sweden" (`script-scene0`, `script-scene3`, `script-scene4`). Note the internal tension: "independent research" (`script-scene4`) versus "in cooperation with" on the same slide.
- **`Correlations for pressure drop and heat transfer.pptx`.** The only source giving usable closed-form fits: a regime-split Nusselt correlation for the finned collector (laminar branch to Re 1700 with a Re^1.77·Pr^0.5 term; transition branch 0.86·(Re−1699)^0.39·Pr^0.32, blended with the smooth laminar Nu) and a logistic-blended friction factor between 64/Re and a Haaland-type term over 1700–2300 (`formula-nu`, `formula-f`). These are **fitted correlations to DNS points**, benchmarked against Gnielinski and Haaland — useful for implementing the effect in a design tool, not independent validation.

---

## 3. Assessment of value beyond ordinary Claude

**(a) General engineering — little to no added value.** Ground properties, R_b decomposition, grout vs groundwater, laminar/turbulent trade-off and TRT procedure are textbook. The baseline answered Q01–Q05 at high confidence and largely correctly. The corpus adds *pedagogical framing and Nordic practice colour* rather than facts a competent engineer lacks: the illustrative sensitivities (1 °C colder ⇒ 10% more borehole, `tr-02-006`), the "20 m ⇒ thermally independent" convention with its honest caveat (`tr-07-003`), the freezing-diagnostics triad (`tr-06-005`–`tr-06-008`), and the TRT qualification that one should match design flow conditions rather than force turbulence (`tr-09-082`). **Confidentiality: low.** This is a lecture by an external expert restating public teaching material.

**(b) Specific research/product information, possibly public.** The DNS study's numbers — alternating helical, 0.6 mm, 16 fins, 360°/0.7 m, unsteady to Re ~1700–1800, +300–600% convective heat transfer over 1700<Re<2300, few-percent-or-less friction penalty outside — are substantive and were entirely absent from the baseline (Q06–Q08 abstained). But the corpus itself says the study is published: "Scientific study … is available online" (`deck-s09`), "it's our secret and … this is public. This is public. This video will be public. Everything we have — that's a requirement for the … consultancy … it needs to be published" (`tr-10-028`), and the lecturer refers to "the recently published paper" (`tr-05-006`). The correlations (`formula-nu`, `formula-f`) and the appendix derivation (`deck-s53`) may or may not be in the public paper — I cannot check. **Confidentiality: low for the headline results; unknown for the fitted correlations and the raw data tables referenced at `tr-10-050`.**

**(c) Record-specific operational information.** Only obtainable from these records: who said what, and the qualifications. Examples: "I cannot say it's an optimum, but it's one of the best" (`tr-10-024`); the untested 2-fin/45°/0.6 mm combination (`tr-10-027`); the lecturer's refusal to quantify SDR 11→13.6 (`tr-09-042`); the unresolved SDR 17 disagreement with Carlos (`tr-09-045`); the tool's 2.5 kPa U-bend allowance, 10% margin, one-way lengths and single-manifold limit (`tr-12-029`–`tr-12-033`). **Confidentiality: mixed.** The engineering qualifications are not obviously sensitive; the tool's internal assumptions plausibly are, until the explanation page is published.

**(d) Commercially sensitive discussion.** Clearly the most distinctive material: extra fin material cost stated as ~3–4% and ~1–2% for halving fin count (`tr-10-029`, `tr-10-041`); "we have different price strategies between the different countries because my turbo price is the same price as my [smooth]" (`tr-10-052`); the rejection of turbo-only production on margin grounds (`tr-10-051`); the named-competitor verdict "anti-turbo… fooling people… most likely a really crappy product" (`tr-10-042`–`tr-10-043`); country die-head variants and the avoided CapEx (`tr-10-022`–`tr-10-023`); the contribution-margin figures and doubling claim (`tr-12-020`); named external tool users harvested for sales follow-up (`tr-12-025`); EUR 25 m turnover 2017 (`deck-s40`). **Confidentiality: this content is sensitive by its nature** — pricing strategy, unit cost, margin, competitor disparagement, and identifiable third-party user data. I do not claim it has never appeared elsewhere. I also do **not** treat `tr-10-028` as a blanket confidentiality marking: the word "secret" is immediately followed by "and … this is public. This is public" in the same turn, so at most it evidences a wish to prepare a coordinated message before external use, not a designation covering the study or the meeting.

---

## 4. Eighteen questions: baseline versus source-backed answer

| Q / topic | Observed baseline | Source-backed answer (citations) | Limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q01 borehole-length drivers | Adequate for core concept | Two dominant properties: undisturbed ground temperature and thermal conductivity (`tr-02-000`). Illustrative: 9 °C/100 m reference; −1 °C ⇒ +10% length; 2 °C ⇒ nearly double (`tr-02-006`). Granite 3.5 W/mK reference; poor granite +20%, best granite −10%, quartzite −20% with drill-bit wear (`tr-02-007`). Only annual **net** extraction per metre drives long-term drift (`tr-07-006`). | Corpus figures are explicitly illustrative; baseline's diffusivity/peak-load point is not in the corpus but is correct. |
| Q02 R_b and collector types | Adequate | R_b = fluid + pipe wall + filling, in series (`tr-03-004`; `deck-s18`). Double-U ≈ half single-U; coaxial ≈ 10× lower (`tr-03-005`). Theoretical example 0.1/0.05/0.01 K·m/W ⇒ 4/2/0.4 K drops at 40 W/m (`tr-03-006`). Cost/reliability favours U-pipe (`tr-03-007`). Crucial caveat: those ratios assume good turbulence in both; badly designed doubles can be worse (`tr-09-046`, `tr-12-020`–`tr-12-021`). | Corpus gives no R_a/short-circuit treatment; baseline's numeric ranges are not corroborated here. |
| Q03 grout vs groundwater | Adequate | Filling provides thermal contact and sealing; grout's main purpose is preventing mixing of waters (`tr-04-000`–`tr-04-001`). Sweden/Norway/Finland and parts of Canada allow open water-filled holes (`tr-04-001`–`tr-04-002`). Stagnant water ≈0.6 W/mK but convection makes effective transport better than cement/graphite (`tr-04-002`). Active length starts at the groundwater surface (`tr-04-004`). Grouted holes should not freeze (`tr-06-000`–`tr-06-001`). | Corpus gives no numeric grout conductivities; ranking is OCR-corroborated but qualitative. |
| Q04 laminar vs turbulent | Adequate | Qualitative mechanism (`tr-05-002`–`tr-05-004`); Re<2300 laminar, ~3000 turbulent, design sits in between (`tr-05-005`); ASHRAE band for SDR 11 (`tr-05-006`). Quantified: brine resistance ~50% of R_b laminar vs ~5% unsteady, 5–10× step (`deck-s19`, `tr-10-004`). | Baseline's Dittus–Boelter/Blasius exponents are not in the corpus; the corpus's fitted correlations (`formula-nu`, `formula-f`) are finned-pipe specific. |
| Q05 TRT | Adequate | Measures effective λ, plus T₀ and R_b as "a bonus" (`tr-08-001`–`tr-08-002`); rig = pump, heater of known capacity, flow meter, inlet/outlet sensors; **≥60 h** (`tr-08-003`); flat curve ⇒ high λ, intercept ⇒ R_b (`tr-08-004`); matters above ~8–10 boreholes (`tr-08-005`); no patent (`tr-08-004`). Nuance: most rigs heat, so it resembles a cooling case (`tr-08-002`); prefer **design** flow conditions over forcing turbulence (`tr-09-082`). DTRT with optical fibre locates fractures (`tr-09-085`). | Corpus says ≥60 h; baseline said 48–72 h. Heating-phase duration in Sweden was asked and **not answered** (`tr-09-086`). |
| Q06 fin geometry | Abstained | Alternating helical fins, **fin height 0.6 mm, 16 fins, 360° twist per ~0.7 m pipe**, pipe inner diameter 40 mm (`tr-10-011`, `tr-10-016`; `deck-s25`, `deck-s30`). >30 designs evaluated (`deck-s30`). | "Promising", not proven optimal (`tr-10-024`). Geometry is the simulated design; production variants differ (180° in Finland, `tr-10-022`). |
| Q07 Reynolds interval and magnitude | Abstained | Largest gain in **1700 < Re < 2300**: +300–600% convective heat transfer vs smooth pipe (`tr-10-019`; `deck-s31`, `deck-s33`). Unsteadiness sustained to ~1700–1800 vs 2300 smooth, i.e. "22% lower flow rates" (`tr-10-012`; `deck-s10`). | DNS only; no experiment. ## 5. Conclusion and next steps

**Where the corpus adds value.** Clearly and only in Q06–Q08 and Q10–Q15, Q17–Q18 — that is, the specific DNS parameters and results, the recorded qualifications around them, and the operational detail of an internal tool and its commercial use. In these the baseline correctly abstained rather than confabulating, which is the right behaviour; the corpus converts eight to ten abstentions into specific, citable answers. Q16 shows the opposite: grounding did **not** produce an answer, because the presupposed event is absent, and the honest output remains an abstention with an explanation of where the neighbouring discussion actually lives.

**Where ordinary Claude is already sufficient.** Q01–Q05. The baseline's answers were adequate for the core concepts and in several respects more systematic than the lectures (diffusivity, shank spacing, correlation exponents). The corpus adds Nordic regulatory context, illustrative sensitivities and two genuine practitioner nuances (TRT at design flow rather than forced turbulence; double-U resistance claims conditional on turbulence). A retrieval layer over this corpus should not be expected to improve fundamentals materially — it should be expected to supply company-specific parameters, recorded caveats and provenance.

**A realistic follow-up study.** To test whether this is a real capability gain rather than an artefact: (i) draft ~30 questions stratified across the four value categories in §3, written without presupposing answers (Q16's flaw); (ii) run matched prompts in three arms — no material, this corpus, and a **public-source comparator** limited to the published Chalmers paper, the MuoviTech website and the public YouTube video — so that "value of the internal records" is separated from "value of any retrieval"; (iii) score blind, by geothermal engineers who do not know the arm, on correctness, citation accuracy, appropriate abstention and unsupported-claim rate; (iv) score abstention positively where evidence is absent, otherwise the design rewards confabulation.

**What this exercise is not.** It is a single, purposive, non-randomised run by the same model that produced the baseline, on a hand-selected corpus, continued across two outputs because of an output-length limit — the continuation boundary alone breaks comparability with a single-pass condition. Full-corpus results are an **upper bound**, not an estimate of production RAG quality: a real system retrieves a handful of chunks, may miss `formula-nu` or `deck-s53` entirely, and will not have the cross-source reconciliation (deck vs narration vs Q&A) that drove several of the qualifications above. Nothing here is an unbiased accuracy benchmark, and none of the transcript figures should enter a specification or brochure without re-reading the slides and the published paper.
